sections.h2: What should you know before selling a house in Wilmington, NC?
sections.html:
Wilmington sellers face a market shaped by water, age and rental demand, so the first step is working out which of those three describes your house. The city sits on the Cape Fear River with the Atlantic to its east, and the city's own overview calls it the eighth largest city in North Carolina, with a population above 120,000 inside a five-county area of more than 484,000.

The Census Bureau puts the July 1, 2025 estimate at 126,809 residents, up 9.8% from the 2020 base, which is fast growth next to most North Carolina cities. A seller here is usually choosing between three routes: a traditional listing with showings and repairs, a sale to an investor or cash buyer who takes the house as it stands, or a hold-and-rent plan. Each one changes how much cash you keep and how soon you get it.

  • List with an agent when the house is in good shape and you can wait through showings and the buyer's inspection and financing.
  • Take a cash offer when repairs, tenants, probate or a looming payment date make time more valuable than the last few percent of price.
  • Rent it out only after checking the city's short-term lodging rules, which are strict for stays of 29 days or less.

sections.h2: What do Census figures say about Wilmington homes and owners?
sections.html:
Wilmington is a renter-heavy, high-priced city by North Carolina standards. The Census Bureau's 2020-2024 figures show 47.6% of homes owner-occupied, a median owner-occupied home value of $383,800 and median gross rent of $1,395.

That gap matters if you inherited a house or own a rental. A large renter base means investors and landlords are a real part of the buyer pool, and a house with a tenant in place can still find a buyer. The same data lists 56,612 households averaging 2.05 people each, and 18.2% of residents are 65 or older. Older owners often face the question of selling a home they no longer want to maintain.

sections.h2: How does Wilmington's location and history affect a house sale?
sections.html:
The river and the coast drive both the economy and the condition of many houses. The city overview describes Wilmington as a port and business center roughly midway along the eastern seaboard, with one of the state's largest historic districts, riverfront walking, nearby beaches and a film industry that uses its varied architecture.

Older neighborhoods near downtown carry the age that buyers either love or discount. If your house is in a historic area, ask the city's planning staff before promising a buyer any exterior change, because the city's permit portal also handles Certificates of Appropriateness.

The city's median commute is short. Census data shows a mean travel time to work of 18.5 minutes, below the 21.3 minutes for Wilson and 21.5 for Winston-Salem in the same table. Census figures for 2022 list health care and social assistance receipts of about $3.2 billion in the city, a sign of how much local work sits outside tourism.

sections.h2: What rules apply if you rent a Wilmington house before selling it?
sections.html:
Wilmington regulates short-term rentals, defined as rentals of 29 days or less, and a seller who has been using a house that way should expect buyers to ask about it. The city splits them into homestay lodging (rooms rented inside the host's principal residence) and whole-house lodging.

  • Homestay: the owner or principal resident must live on site, with at most three guest rooms and one fewer than the bedroom count.
  • Whole-house: no owner occupancy rule, but a local operator must be reachable around the clock and live within 25 miles.
  • Parking: whole-house lodging needs one off-street space per bedroom on an all-weather surface.
  • Insurance: commercial general liability coverage of at least $500,000 per occurrence.
  • No parties, weddings or large gatherings, and a posted notice with host contact details.

Owners register online through the city, and the registration number goes on every listing. Questions go to the city's compliance staff at zoning@wilmingtonnc.gov or 910-254-0900. Ask the compliance office whether a longer lease falls outside these rules before you rely on it.

sections.h2: How do Wilmington permits and open work affect a cash sale?
sections.html:
Any change of use, and any vacancy of more than 180 days, needs a zoning permit under the city's use-permit page, and all new permit applications now go through the city's online Development and Permitting Services portal. If you started a project that was never finished, close the permit before you list.

The city warns on its permit pages that fraudulent invoices have been sent to applicants by email, asking for wire transfers. Real fees appear in your account dashboard on the city portal, and the city says it will never ask for payment by wire. Confirm any invoice with the Planning Department before paying.

Cash buyers normally take a house with open permits, but the price reflects the risk. A permitted, inspected repair is easier to sell than an unpermitted one, so photograph finished work and keep the paperwork.

sections.h2: Who bills property tax on a Wilmington house, and what are the rates?
sections.html:
New Hanover County bills the tax, and the bill also carries the City of Wilmington's levy. A July 2026 county notice says the county rate is set at 30.6 cents per $100 for fiscal year 2026-2027, with the City of Wilmington at 33.15 cents and the City of Wilmington Municipal Services District at 5 cents. Carolina Beach, Kure Beach and Wrightsville Beach have their own rates on the same notice. Ask the tax office to confirm the figures for the year you close.

The county mailed bills in July, with taxes due September 1 and payable without interest into early January. The notice says the bill includes four payment coupons that split the total into four equal payments. Owners paying through escrow get a courtesy notice and should verify with their lender that payment went out.

The county tax office is at the Government Center in Wilmington, with a drop box by the main entrance, and answers questions at (910) 798-7300.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Wilmington assessment?
sections.html:
You appeal to the New Hanover County Tax Administrator first, then to the Board of Equalization and Review. The county asks owners to file within 30 days of the notice so staff can attempt an informal fix, but every appeal must arrive electronically or be postmarked by the board's adjournment date. For the 2026 tax year that date was May 14, 2026, so that window has closed; the next one will come after the next notice.

The county's last revaluation measured value as of January 1, 2025. State law requires each county to reappraise every eight years, and a larger county can be forced to move sooner if its sales ratio drifts out of range. The board mails its written decision within 30 days after it meets, and a further appeal goes to the Property Tax Commission within 30 days of that notice.

  • Gather recent sales of comparable houses and any appraisal.
  • Document condition problems such as roof, flood or foundation damage.
  • Individual owners may represent themselves; business entities and non-owners face rules on who can speak for them.

sections.h2: What closing costs and tax relief should a Wilmington seller expect?
sections.html:
The seller pays North Carolina's deed excise tax, which the statute sets at $1.00 for each $500 of consideration or fraction of it, paid to the register of deeds before recording. Recording fees are set statewide: $26 for the first 15 pages of an ordinary instrument and $64 for a mortgage or deed of trust, with $4 for each added page.

Older or disabled owners, and disabled veterans, may have lower tax bills. The elderly or disabled exclusion removes the greater of $25,000 or half the appraised value of a residence, the disabled veteran exclusion covers the first $45,000, and the circuit breaker caps tax at 4% or 5% of income and defers the rest as a lien. Deferred tax comes due when the owner sells, so a sale triggers repayment. File through the county tax office by June 1 each year; the state allows only one of these three benefits per owner.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Wilmington house without making repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash buyer or investor can buy as-is, and a traditional buyer may accept the house if the price reflects its condition. Expect an inspection either way. Open permits and unfinished work should be disclosed and, where possible, closed.

faqs.q: Do Wilmington's short-term rental rules follow the house to a new owner?
faqs.a: The city requires the owner to register each lodging property and put the registration number in every listing. Ask the city's compliance staff whether a registration transfers or must be filed again by the buyer.

faqs.q: Who pays the property tax bill if I sell in the middle of the year?
faqs.a: Tax is billed to the owner on January 1, and the buyer and seller usually split it at closing. New Hanover County bills are due September 1 and payable without interest into early January. Ask your closing attorney to show the proration and pay any unpaid bill at closing.

faqs.q: What does it cost to record a deed in New Hanover County?
faqs.a: The seller pays the state excise tax of $1.00 per $500 of value. Recording a standard instrument costs $26 for the first 15 pages under G.S. 161-10, and a deed of trust costs $64 for its first 35 pages. The register of deeds collects both before recording.

faqs.q: Where do I ask about my Wilmington tax assessment?
faqs.a: Contact the New Hanover County Tax Department at (910) 798-7300. The 2026 appeal deadline of May 14, 2026 has passed, so watch for the next assessment notice and file by the board's adjournment date in that year.
